options: A predicate shaped so the optimizer can use an index seek directly, without evaluating a function per row
A query that always returns fewer than 100 rows
A synonym for a covering index
A predicate that always uses a table hint
questions.explain: Sargable (Search ARGument ABLE) describes a predicate the optimizer can satisfy via an index seek rather than a full scan.

questions.q: Why does `WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026` typically prevent an index seek on OrderDate?
options: Wrapping the column in a function means SQL Server must compute that function for every row before it can filter, forcing a scan instead of a seek
YEAR() is not a valid T-SQL function
It actually does seek the index just as efficiently as a range predicate
OrderDate columns can never be indexed
questions.explain: Wrapping an indexed column in a function makes the predicate non-sargable — the optimizer can't determine which index entries match without evaluating the function per row.

questions.q: What is the sargable rewrite of `WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026` shown in this lesson?
options: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2027-01-01'
WHERE OrderDate = 2026
WHERE CONVERT(int, OrderDate) = 2026
WHERE OrderDate LIKE '2026%'
questions.explain: A plain range predicate directly on the raw OrderDate column lets the optimizer seek the index, returning the same result set as the function-wrapped version.

questions.q: How can an implicit conversion silently turn a seek into a scan, per this lesson?
options: Comparing a column to a literal of a different data type can force SQL Server to convert the column's value on every row, depending on data type precedence rules, with no function visibly wrapping the column
Implicit conversions are resolved entirely at compile time and never affect execution
Implicit conversions only occur when using CAST or CONVERT explicitly
They only affect columnstore indexes, never rowstore indexes
questions.explain: Comparing an nvarchar column to an int literal, for example, can force a per-row conversion on the column side, silently defeating a seek without any visible function call.

questions.q: Beyond readability, what real performance cost can SELECT * introduce?
options: It can defeat a covering index built for the query's actual needed columns, forcing a Key Lookup or wider scan, and increases data transferred over the network
It always causes a syntax error in SQL Server
It forces the query to run under READ UNCOMMITTED isolation
It has no measurable performance impact in any scenario
questions.explain: Selecting every column defeats a narrowly built covering index and moves more data than necessary across the network on each execution.
